etymology: The second-person singular present of go, formed with the Old English ending -est. Webster 1828 lists it as the archaic inflection used with thou. Its presence in the Authorized Version is not ornament: it marks that one person, not a crowd, is being addressed.
biblical_def: Goest is the form go takes when God or a man speaks to a single person, and the Authorized Version preserves a distinction modern English has lost. Every thou…goest in Scripture is a promise or a demand aimed at one man. God says to Jacob, alone on a stone at Bethel with his brother behind him and a stranger’s house ahead, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land (Genesis 28:15). To Joshua, standing where Moses had stood, the same singular: be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest (Joshua 1:9). The command to be strong is not general encouragement broadcast to a nation; it is laid on one man’s shoulders with a promise attached to his particular movements. Ruth uses the form to bind herself to Naomi: whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God (Ruth 1:16) — a covenant made by a Moabitess to a bereaved woman with nothing to give her. And a would-be disciple offers it to Christ without counting what it costs: Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest (Luke 9:57), to which the Lord answered that the Son of man had nowhere to lay His head.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 treats GOEST as the second person singular of the verb go, used with the pronoun thou: thou goest, that is, thou movest, walkest, passest, or proceedest from one place to another.
webster_full: GOEST — the second person singular, present tense, of the verb GO; used with the pronoun thou.
GO, v.i. — To move, to pass, to proceed from one place, condition, or state to another.
To walk; to move on the feet, as distinguished from riding or being carried.
To depart; to set out on a journey or course; as, whither goest thou?
From Saxon gan, to go — the root also of gone, gait, and gang in its older English sense of going.
scriptures: Genesis 28:15

And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land; for I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of.
Joshua 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Ruth 1:16

And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
Luke 9:57
And it came to pass, that, as they went in the way, a certain man said unto him, Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.
corruption_summary: Modern English has collapsed the singular thou and the plural ye into one word, and every translation that follows it silently destroys information the Hebrew and Greek carry, so that readers cannot tell whether a promise or a command lands on one person or on the whole congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: The loss is not sentimental. In the Authorized Version thou, thee, thy and the verb ending -est are always singular, while ye, you and your are always plural, and the translators used them with mechanical consistency to reproduce a distinction present in both Hebrew and Greek. When Joshua 1:9 says whithersoever thou goest, the reader of the AV knows the promise is to Joshua personally. When the Lord tells Peter Simon, Simon, Satan hath desired to have you and then I have prayed for thee, the AV shows what a modern version cannot: Satan asked for all the disciples, Christ prayed for one man by name. A version that renders both with you has not modernised the sentence; it has deleted the point of it.

The usual reply is that thou is archaic and therefore a barrier, but the archaism is doing work no living English form can do, and the argument proves more than its makers want. The same reasoning would strip the covenant name, the imprecatory psalms, and the genealogies. The dictionary does not hold that the AV’s English is inspired or that other faithful translations may not be used; it holds that where a version discards a distinction the original languages actually make, the reader is poorer and usually does not know it. Recovering the second-person singular forms is one of the plainest arguments for keeping the Authorized Version in the hands of the people who study.
roots_summary: Hebrew halak (H1980), to go, to walk, to proceed; yatsa (H3318), to go out; Greek poreuomai (G4198), to go, to journey; hupago (G5217), to go away, to depart.
roots_lines: Hebrew halak (H1980) — to go, to walk; the great Old Testament verb of both travel and moral conduct (Genesis 28:15; Micah 6:8).
Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — to go out, go forth; used of armies, of the word of the LORD, and of a man leaving his house.
Greek poreuomai (G4198) — to go, to proceed, to journey; whithersoever thou goest (Luke 9:57).
Greek hupago (G5217) — to withdraw, to go away; the Lord’s word for His own departure to the Father (John 16:5).
Greek peripateo (G4043) — to walk about; the New Testament equivalent of halak in its moral sense (Ephesians 4:1).
usage: I will keep thee in all places whither thou goest (Genesis 28:15) — a promise to one fugitive man.
The LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest (Joshua 1:9) — the courage commanded rests on the presence promised.
Whither thou goest, I will go (Ruth 1:16) — a Moabitess binding herself to Israel’s God.

etymology: The second-person singular present of do, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 records it as the form used with thou, distinguishing it from the third-person doeth. Matthew 6:3 sets the two side by side in a single sentence.
biblical_def: Doest is what a man is asked about when God addresses him singly, and Scripture uses it to press the question of conduct onto one conscience at a time. The Lord attributes the form to God Himself in the psalmist’s praise: Thou art good, and doest good; teach me thy statutes (Psalm 119:68) — goodness of nature and goodness of action joined, so that what God does may be trusted because of what God is. Christ uses the form to govern the whole practice of almsgiving: But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth (Matthew 6:3). The singular is essential; giving is examined man by man, and the second half of the verse deliberately shifts to the third person doeth to make the point that even the giver’s own reckoning of his generosity is to be kept quiet. Elihu presses the question of whether human sin can touch God: If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him? (Job 35:6) — not that sin is trivial but that it injures the sinner, not the Almighty. Nicodemus grants what the miracles prove: no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him (John 3:2). And Ecclesiastes shows the form used of an absolute earthly power: who may say unto him, What doest thou? (Ecclesiastes 8:4).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives DOEST as the second person singular of the verb do, used with thou: to perform, to execute, to practise, to bring to pass. Webster notes the distinction between doest (second person) and doeth (third person), both of which the Authorized Version observes exactly.
webster_full: DOEST — the second person singular, present tense, of the verb DO; used with the pronoun thou.
DO, v.t. — To perform; to execute; to carry into effect; to bring to pass.
To practise or commit, as an act, whether good or evil; as, to do justice, to do wrong.
To finish; to complete; whence the participle done, signifying finished or ended.
From Saxon don, to do — distinguished from doeth, the third person singular, which the Authorized Version keeps distinct throughout.
scriptures: Psalm 119:68
Thou art good, and doest good; teach me thy statutes.
Matthew 6:3
But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:
Job 35:6
If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him?
John 3:2
The same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him.
Ecclesiastes 8:4
Where the word of a king is, there is power: and who may say unto him, What doest thou?
corruption_summary: Matthew 6:3 forbids the publicising of one’s own giving, and the modern practice of named donor tiers, publicised pledges, and ministry generosity campaigns runs against the plain sense of a command the Lord gave in the singular.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord’s instruction is stricter than the way it is usually softened. He does not say give without boasting; He says let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth, which forbids even the giver’s settled internal accounting of his own generosity, and He grounds it on the Father seeing in secret. Against that, the donor wall, the named seat, the pledge card read aloud, and the campaign that publishes giving levels are not neutral fundraising mechanics; they are the reward taken in advance, which is exactly the transaction Christ describes in Matthew 6:2 with the word verily I say unto you, They have their reward. A church may keep the records its officers need without turning giving into a public league table.

Psalm 119:68 guards the other flank. Because God is good, what He does is good, and the psalmist draws the practical conclusion in the same breath: teach me thy statutes. The modern instinct runs the other way, judging God’s character by whether His providences appear good to us, so that a hard year becomes evidence against His goodness. Job 35:6 punctures the related conceit that our conduct alters God’s condition. Sin ruins the sinner and offends infinite majesty; it does not wound God as a man is wounded. Holding both verses together yields the Reformed instinct in practice: God’s goodness is the fixed point from which providence is read, not the variable that providence adjusts.
roots_summary: Hebrew asah (H6213), to do, make, accomplish; paal (H6466), to work, to do; Greek poieo (G4160), to do, to make; prasso (G4238), to practise, to perform habitually.
roots_lines: Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, to make; the commonest Old Testament verb of action, used of God’s creating and of man’s obeying.
Hebrew paal (H6466) — to work, to do; often of deliberate workmanship, and of the workers of iniquity.
Greek poieo (G4160) — to do, to make; when thou doest alms (Matthew 6:3) and these miracles that thou doest (John 3:2).
Greek prasso (G4238) — to practise, to do repeatedly; the verb of habitual conduct (Romans 1:32; John 3:20).
Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to work, to labour; work out your own salvation stands nearby in Philippians 2:12.
usage: Thou art good, and doest good (Psalm 119:68) — the acts follow the nature.
When thou doest alms (Matthew 6:3) — giving examined one conscience at a time.
What doest thou against him? (Job 35:6) — sin ruins the sinner, it does not injure God.

etymology: The second-person singular present of see, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 records it as the form used with thou. In the prophetic books it is God’s own question to His prophet — what seest thou? — and the answer is always a plain object, never an impression.
biblical_def: Seest carries a striking weight in Scripture because God repeatedly asks it of His prophets, and the answers are the most sober thing about biblical prophecy. Jeremiah, what seest thou? And I said, I see a rod of an almond tree (Jeremiah 1:11) — an ordinary branch, and from it the pun that God will hasten His word to perform it. To Amos the same question and an equally plain answer: Amos, what seest thou? And I said, A plumbline (Amos 7:8), followed by the sentence that God will set a plumbline in the midst of His people and pass by them no more. The prophets do not report ecstasies; they report objects, and God supplies the interpretation. The form also marks the gift of land by sight: For all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever (Genesis 13:15), spoken to Abram after Lot had chosen the well-watered plain, so that the man who yielded the better ground was given the whole horizon. And the risen Christ commands John to write what he actually sees, not what he devises: What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia (Revelation 1:11). Revelation is given, seen, and recorded; at no point in the chain is it invented.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives SEEST as the second person singular of the verb see, used with thou: to perceive by the eye; to behold; to discern; to understand. Webster notes the extended senses of perceiving by the mind and of being present as a witness.
webster_full: SEEST — the second person singular, present tense, of the verb SEE; used with the pronoun thou.
SEE, v.t. — To perceive by the eye; to behold; to have knowledge of the existence and apparent qualities of objects by the organs of sight.
To discern; to distinguish; to perceive intellectually; as, I see the force of the argument.
To attend; to be present as a spectator or witness; and hence, to experience, as to see death.
From Saxon seon, to see — the root also of seer, one who sees, the older English word for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9).
scriptures: Jeremiah 1:11
Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, Jeremiah, what seest thou? And I said, I see a rod of an almond tree.
Amos 7:8
And the LORD said unto me, Amos, what seest thou? And I said, A plumbline. Then said the Lord, Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more:
Genesis 13:15
For all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever.
Revelation 1:11

Saying, I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last: and, What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia; unto Ephesus, and unto Smyrna, and unto Pergamos, and unto Thyatira, and unto Sardis, and unto Philadelphia, and unto Laodicea.
corruption_summary: Modern charismatic practice has replaced the prophet’s plain object with the believer’s inward impression, so that I see now introduces a picture in the mind offered as a word from God, with no test, no object, and no accountability when it fails.
corruption_paragraphs: Set Jeremiah 1:11 beside the contemporary prophetic word and the difference is total. God asks Jeremiah what he sees; Jeremiah names a branch of an almond tree; God supplies the meaning and the meaning is a threat of judgment the prophet then delivers under penalty of death if it proves false (Deuteronomy 18:20-22). Amos sees a plumbline and is told Israel will not be spared again. In each case the object is external and public, the interpretation is God’s, and the prophet is answerable. Where I see now introduces an impression arising in a believer’s own imagination, offered without falsifiable content and revised when circumstances disappoint, none of the biblical safeguards apply, and the name of the LORD is attached to a guess.

Revelation 1:11 sets the standard the church should hold: What thou seest, write in a book. The vision is given, John records it, and the record is closed and public. The dictionary’s position is cessationist in the confessional sense that no revelation is now given which binds the conscience or adds to Scripture, and Revelation 22:18-19 pronounces a curse on additions to this particular book. That is not a denial that God providentially guides His people or impresses duties upon them by the Word; it is a refusal to let an impression be dressed as revelation. Genesis 13:15 shows the other, older use of the word, and it rebukes covetousness: Abram was given all he could see precisely after letting Lot take what looked better.
roots_summary: Hebrew raah (H7200), to see, to look, to perceive; chazah (H2372), to see in vision, whence chazon, a vision; Greek blepo (G991), to see, to look at; horao (G3708), to see, to perceive.
roots_lines: Hebrew raah (H7200) — to see, to look; also roeh, a seer, the older title for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9).
Hebrew chazah (H2372) — to see, especially in prophetic vision; the root of chazon, the vision of Isaiah and of Nahum.
Greek blepo (G991) — to see with the eyes, to look at; What thou seest, write in a book (Revelation 1:11).
Greek horao (G3708) — to see, to discern, to experience; behind they shall see God (Matthew 5:8).
Greek optasia (G3701) — a vision, an appearance; used of Zacharias in the temple (Luke 1:22).
usage: Jeremiah, what seest thou? (Jeremiah 1:11) — God’s question, and a plain object for an answer.
All the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it (Genesis 13:15) — the whole horizon given to the man who yielded the better ground.
What thou seest, write in a book (Revelation 1:11) — revelation given, recorded, and closed.

etymology: The second-person singular past of give, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it as the form used with thou. In John 17 the word occurs repeatedly of the Father’s giving of a particular people to the Son, and the repetition is the backbone of the chapter.
biblical_def: Gavest is the word on which the seventeenth chapter of John turns, and the doctrine it carries is definite redemption. Christ prays: I have manifested thy name unto the men which thou gavest me out of the world: thine they were, and thou gavest them me; and they have kept thy word (John 17:6). Three clauses, and each one narrows: a particular company, given out of the world rather than identical with it, belonging to the Father before they were given. The Lord had already stated the finished work in the same terms: I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do (John 17:4), and the work given was the work completed — not offered, not attempted. The same form appears in the first evasion in human history, where Adam turns God’s gift into God’s fault: The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat (Genesis 3:12). The grammar blames the Giver. And Nehemiah’s great prayer of national confession uses the form to rehearse mercies received: And gavest them bread from heaven for their hunger, and broughtest forth water for them out of the rock for their thirst (Nehemiah 9:15). Whether in the mouth of the Son, the sinner, or the penitent nation, gavest always locates the giving in God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives GAVEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb give, used with thou: to bestow, to confer without price, to grant, to deliver over, to yield.
webster_full: GAVEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb GIVE; used with the pronoun thou.
GIVE, v.t. — To bestow; to confer; to pass or transfer the property of a thing to another person without an equivalent.
To grant; to allow; to yield; as, to give consent, or to give place.
To deliver over; to commit to another’s trust or charge; as, the work which thou gavest me to do.
From Saxon gifan, to give — the root also of gift, forgive, and given.
scriptures: John 17:6
I have manifested thy name unto the men which thou gavest me out of the world: thine they were, and thou gavest them me; and they have kept thy word.
John 17:4
I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.
Genesis 3:12
And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.
Nehemiah 9:15

And gavest them bread from heaven for their hunger, and broughtest forth water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and promisedst them that they should go in to possess the land which thou hadst sworn to give them.
corruption_summary: Universal-atonement teaching requires John 17 to mean that the Father gave the Son every human being without exception, which the chapter itself refuses in the next breath: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me.
corruption_paragraphs: John 17:9 is the verse that decides the matter, and it is decided by the Lord Jesus in prayer, which is the least polemical setting imaginable. I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine. If the given ones were all men without exception, the sentence contradicts itself, since the world would then be the same company He declines to pray for. The Arminian reading must therefore make the giving conditional on foreseen faith, but John 17:6 says thine they were, and thou gavest them me — they belonged to the Father before the giving, and the keeping of the word follows rather than precedes it. Owen’s argument in The Death of Death is simply this chapter pressed: the Intercessor prays for exactly those for whom He died.

Genesis 3:12 names a corruption older than any doctrinal system and more common than all of them. Adam does not deny the act; he redistributes the blame with perfect grammatical precision — the woman whom thou gavest to be with me — implicating his wife in the first clause and God in the relative clause. Every excuse since has followed the pattern, tracing sin backward through circumstance to the Giver of the circumstance. The therapeutic vocabulary of environment, conditioning, and the wounds one has sustained is the same move with better manners, and it is answered the same way: God asked Adam what he had done, not what had been done to him.
roots_summary: Hebrew nathan (H5414), to give, to set, to appoint; Greek didomi (G1325), to give; paradidomi (G3860), to deliver over, to hand across; doron (G1435), a gift.
roots_lines: Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give, put, appoint; over two thousand occurrences, from the giving of the land to the giving of a heart of flesh.
Greek didomi (G1325) — to give; the verb of John 17:6, and of God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to deliver over; used both of the Father delivering up the Son (Romans 8:32) and of Judas betraying Him.
Greek doron (G1435) — a gift, an offering; not of works, lest any man should boast stands beside it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8-9).
Greek charizomai (G5483) — to give freely as a favour; formed from charis, grace.
usage: The men which thou gavest me out of the world (John 17:6) — a particular people, given before they believed.
I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do (John 17:4) — the work given was the work completed.
The woman whom thou gavest to be with me (Genesis 3:12) — the first excuse, and it blames the Giver.

etymology: The second-person singular past of come, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it as the form used with thou. In John 16:30 it carries the disciples’ confession of the Lord’s pre-existence and mission, and in Genesis 16:8 it is the question the angel asks a runaway slave.
biblical_def: Camest appears at some of Scripture’s most searching moments, because to ask a person where he came from is to ask what he is doing. The angel of the LORD finds Hagar by a fountain in the wilderness and asks the two questions that expose her whole situation: Hagar, Sarai’s maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? (Genesis 16:8). She can answer the first and not the second, which is the condition of every runaway. Eliab uses the form as a weapon against his younger brother: Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? (1 Samuel 17:28) — contempt disguised as concern for duty, spoken to the one man in the camp who was about to act. Ananias uses it to name the encounter on the Damascus road: the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight (Acts 9:17), and the word brother that opens the sentence is one of the great small mercies of Scripture. Highest of all, the disciples use the form to confess the Lord’s origin: by this we believe that thou camest forth from God (John 16:30) — not that He was sent as prophets are sent, but that He came forth from the Father, which is the confession the whole Gospel of John is written to produce.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives CAMEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb come, used with thou: to move toward, to approach, to arrive, to proceed or issue from.
webster_full: CAMEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb COME; used with the pronoun thou.
COME, v.i. — To move toward; to advance nearer, in any manner, and from any distance.
To arrive, as at some place or state; as, the letter is come; the time is come.
To proceed or issue from; as, wine comes from the grape; and in Scripture, to come forth from God.
From Saxon cuman, to come — the root also of became, welcome, and income.
scriptures: Genesis 16:8
And he said, Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? And she said, I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai.
1 Samuel 17:28

And Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spake unto the men; and Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle.
Acts 9:17

And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost.
John 16:30
Now are we sure that thou knowest all things, and needest not that any man should ask thee: by this we believe that thou camest forth from God.
corruption_summary: John 16:30 confesses that Christ came forth from God before He came into the world, and every adoptionist and merely-human account of Jesus — ancient Ebionite, Socinian, nineteenth-century liberal, or modern historical-Jesus reconstruction — must empty the verb of its origin.
corruption_paragraphs: To say that Christ came forth from God is to say He was with God before He came, and John states it flatly at the head of the Gospel: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The adoptionist alternative — that a man was raised to divine sonship at his baptism or resurrection — was condemned in the second century, revived by the Socinians, and is the working assumption of most reconstructions of a Jesus behind the Gospels. The dictionary names it as error rather than as an alternative reading. John 16:28 gives the full arc in the Lord’s own words: I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father. A merely human Jesus has nowhere to come from and nowhere to return to.

Genesis 16:8 supplies the pastoral counterpart. God knows Hagar’s name, her station, and her mistress before He speaks, and He asks anyway, because the question is for her. She answers honestly about the flight and says nothing about the destination, since she had none. The Lord then sends her back to a hard house with a promise attached, and she names Him Thou God seest me. It is worth setting that against the modern counsel that would have confirmed her in the escape. Scripture’s mercy to the mistreated is real — the angel found her, not Sarai — but it does not consist in ratifying the flight; it consists in a promise large enough to make return bearable.
roots_summary: Hebrew bo (H935), to come, to go in, to enter; yatsa (H3318), to go out, to come forth; Greek erchomai (G2064), to come, to go; exerchomai (G1831), to come forth, to proceed out from.
roots_lines: Hebrew bo (H935) — to come in, to enter; used of Noah entering the ark and of the LORD coming to His temple.
Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — to go out, come forth; behind out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel (Micah 5:2).
Greek erchomai (G2064) — to come; the verb of the Lord’s advent and of His promised return.
Greek exerchomai (G1831) — to come forth out of; thou camest forth from God (John 16:30).
Greek heko (G2240) — to have come, to be present; Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me (Hebrews 10:7).
usage: Whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? (Genesis 16:8) — the two questions that expose a runaway.
Why camest thou down hither? (1 Samuel 17:28) — contempt dressed as concern for duty.
Thou camest forth from God (John 16:30) — the confession the Gospel of John was written to produce.

etymology: The second-person singular past of say, with the Old English -est ending contracted. Webster 1828 lists saidst and saidest as the forms used with thou. Its most important use in Scripture is in prayer, where a man quotes God’s own word back to Him.
biblical_def: Saidst is the word of a man holding God to what God has spoken, and Scripture treats that as the highest kind of praying rather than presumption. Jacob, terrified on the night before Esau met him, does not plead his own record; he pleads the promise: And thou saidst, I will surely do thee good, and make thy seed as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude (Genesis 32:12). He has just confessed himself unworthy of the least of God’s mercies, and then quotes the covenant word back with thou saidst. David does the same with an invitation: When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek (Psalm 27:8) — the command becomes the warrant for the obedience, and the answer is framed as an echo. The form is also used to convict. Abimelech confronts Isaac with his own words about Rebekah: how saidst thou, She is my sister? (Genesis 26:9), and a pagan king rebukes a patriarch for a lie learned from his father. Zebul flings Gaal’s boast back at him: Where is now thy mouth, wherewith thou saidst, Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? (Judges 9:38). A man’s words are kept, and he will meet them again.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives SAIDST (also SAIDEST) as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb say, used with thou: to speak, to utter in words, to declare, to affirm.
webster_full: SAIDST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb SAY; used with the pronoun thou.
SAY, v.t. — To speak; to utter in words; to declare or affirm in speech.
To allege by way of argument or excuse; as, what sayest thou for thyself?
To pronounce or repeat, as a set form of words; as, to say a lesson or to say grace.
From Saxon secgan, to say — the root also of saw in the old sense of a saying, and of soothsay.
scriptures: Genesis 32:12
And thou saidst, I will surely do thee good, and make thy seed as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude.
Psalm 27:8
When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek.
Genesis 26:9
And Abimelech called Isaac, and said, Behold, of a surety she is thy wife: and how saidst thou, She is my sister? And Isaac said unto him, Because I said, Lest I die for her.
Judges 9:38

Then said Zebul unto him, Where is now thy mouth, wherewith thou saidst, Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? is not this the people that thou hast despised? go out, I pray now, and fight with them.
corruption_summary: Word-of-faith teaching has seized the pattern of pleading God’s word and inverted it, so that the believer’s confession is said to create the reality rather than to lay hold of what God has already promised.
corruption_paragraphs: The difference between Jacob at Peniel and the modern positive confession is the difference between a promise and an incantation. Jacob quotes a word God actually spoke to him at Bethel and in Genesis 31:3, and he quotes it while confessing I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies. He is not generating an outcome; he is holding a covenant God to a covenant word, which is the whole logic of Reformed prayer. Word-of-faith teaching — Kenyon, Hagin, Copeland and their successors — instead makes the spoken confession the operative force, so that health and wealth are released by declaring them and withheld by admitting difficulty. That doctrine cannot survive Genesis 32, where the man who prays this way spends the night wrestling and walks away permanently lamed.

Genesis 26:9 and Judges 9:38 name the corruption on the human side, and it is simply the assumption that words evaporate. Isaac repeats his father’s lie about his wife and is rebuked by a Philistine king; Gaal’s boast is quoted back to him on the morning he must fight. Christ said that every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment (Matthew 12:36), which is the same principle raised to its final court. In an age of untracked speech and disposable public statements, the biblical assumption — that what a man said is preserved and will be produced — is worth recovering as a discipline of the tongue.
roots_summary: Hebrew amar (H559), to say, to speak, to command; dabar (H1696), to speak, whence dabar, a word or thing; Greek lego (G3004), to say; epo (G2036), the aorist, to speak.
roots_lines: Hebrew amar (H559) — to say; the verb of And God said, Let there be light and of every thus saith the LORD.
Hebrew dabar (H1696) — to speak; its noun dabar means both word and thing, since God’s speech is deed.
Greek lego (G3004) — to say, to lay out in words; the ordinary New Testament verb of speech.
Greek epo (G2036) — the aorist of lego; behind the repeated he said of the Gospels.
Hebrew neum (H5002) — an utterance, an oracle; the solemn saith the LORD that seals a prophetic word.
usage: And thou saidst, I will surely do thee good (Genesis 32:12) — a man pleading God’s own promise back to Him.
When thou saidst, Seek ye my face (Psalm 27:8) — the command becomes the warrant for the obedience.
How saidst thou, She is my sister? (Genesis 26:9) — a man met by his own words in another man’s mouth.

etymology: The second-person singular past of see, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it as the form used with thou. Daniel and Revelation use it repeatedly as the hinge between vision and interpretation: thou sawest… and then the meaning.
biblical_def: Sawest is the word by which an interpreter takes hold of what another man has seen and tells him what it was. Daniel uses it to recount Nebuchadnezzar’s dream before explaining it: Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image. This great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee; and the form thereof was terrible (Daniel 2:31). Daniel had not been told the dream; God gave him both the vision and its meaning, which is why the chapter proves the God of heaven against the wise men of Babylon. The decisive clause follows: Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces (Daniel 2:34) — a kingdom not raised by human hands that shatters the succession of empires. Revelation uses the form the same way as the angel interprets to John: the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings, which have received no kingdom as yet (Revelation 17:12). And Jonathan uses it to plead David’s cause before Saul, appealing to what his father had seen with his own eyes: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause? (1 Samuel 19:5). Seeing binds a man; he cannot afterward act as though he had not seen.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives SAWEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb see, used with thou: didst behold, didst perceive by the eye, didst witness.
webster_full: SAWEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb SEE; used with the pronoun thou.
SEE, v.t. — To perceive by the eye; to behold; and in the past, to have beheld or witnessed.
To have known by observation or experience; as, thou sawest it, and didst rejoice.
In prophetic narrative, to have beheld in vision that which God presented to the mind.
From Saxon seon, to see; the past tense saw, with the second person singular ending -est.
scriptures: Daniel 2:31
Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image. This great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee; and the form thereof was terrible.
Daniel 2:34
Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces.
Revelation 17:12
And the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings, which have received no kingdom as yet; but receive power as kings one hour with the beast.
1 Samuel 19:5

For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?
corruption_summary: The late-dating of Daniel to the second century BC is not a conclusion drawn from the text but a requirement imposed by the assumption that predictive prophecy cannot happen, and it is the standard critical position taught in most universities and many seminaries.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument runs backwards from a premise. Daniel 2 and Daniel 7-11 describe the succession of empires with an accuracy that grows sharper as it approaches the Greek period, so the critical school concludes that the book must have been written after those events, around 165 BC, by an author writing history as though it were prophecy. But the accuracy is the datum, and the second-century date is the device for removing it. The dictionary holds the sixth-century date and Danielic authorship. The Lord Jesus cited Daniel the prophet by name (Matthew 24:15); the book was already in the Greek Old Testament translated in the third and second centuries; and the theory requires that a pseudonymous work produced within living memory be received as ancient Scripture by the very generation that would have known better.

What is at stake is not a date but whether God announces the future. Daniel 2:34 shows a stone cut out without hands smashing the image and becoming a mountain that fills the earth — the kingdom of God set up in the days of those kings and never destroyed. Isaiah makes prediction the very proof of deity: shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods (Isaiah 41:23). A method that rules out predictive prophecy before reading the text has decided the question of God before opening the book, and it will produce a late date for every passage that foretells anything. 1 Samuel 19:5 supplies the other application: Saul had seen David’s deliverance of Israel and rejoiced in it, and Jonathan holds him to it — envy requires a man to un-see what he has seen.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazah (H2372), to see in vision; raah (H7200), to see, to behold; Aramaic chaza (H2370), to see, the verb of Daniel’s Aramaic chapters; Greek eido (G1492), to see, to know.
roots_lines: Aramaic chaza (H2370) — to see, to behold; the verb of Daniel 2:31 and 2:34 in the Aramaic section of the book.
Hebrew chazah (H2372) — to see in vision; the root of chozeh, a seer, and chazon, a vision.
Hebrew raah (H7200) — to see, to look upon; used of ordinary sight and of prophetic sight alike.
Greek eido (G1492) — to see and thereby to know; behind the repeated which thou sawest of Revelation 17.
Greek apokalupsis (G602) — an uncovering, a revelation; the title of the last book and the thing seeing yields.
usage: Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image (Daniel 2:31) — the dream recounted by a man who was never told it.
Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands (Daniel 2:34) — the kingdom no human hand erects.
Thou sawest it, and didst rejoice (1 Samuel 19:5) — envy requires a man to un-see what he has seen.

etymology: The second-person singular past of may, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it among the forms of may used with thou. In Scripture it almost always introduces a purpose clause: God did this that thou mightest do or know that.
biblical_def: Mightest is a purpose word, and the purposes it introduces are among the plainest statements in Scripture of why God does what He does. At Sinai’s aftermath Moses tells Israel the reason for the whole terrifying display: Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him (Deuteronomy 4:35). The revelation was not given to produce awe as an end in itself but knowledge of the one God, and the monotheism of Israel is grounded on demonstration rather than speculation. Luke opens his Gospel with the same construction: That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed (Luke 1:4) — the aim of an orderly written account is certainty, which is a striking claim for a book so often read as though certainty were beyond it. Ananias states the purpose of his errand to a blind persecutor: hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost (Acts 9:17). And Paul charges Timothy with the purpose of the prophecies spoken over him: that thou by them mightest war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18) — gifts and prophecies given not for the man’s comfort but for his campaign.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives MIGHTEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the auxiliary verb MAY, used with thou: expressing possibility, liberty, or purpose — that thou mightest know, that is, in order that thou shouldest be able to know.
webster_full: MIGHTEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the auxiliary verb MAY; used with the pronoun thou.
MAY, aux. v. — To be possible; to express liberty, permission, or opportunity.
In the past tense, used to express the end or purpose of an action; as, this was done that thou mightest know.
Also expressing wish or desire; as, might it be so; and in Scripture, the design of God in a providence.
From Saxon magan, to be able — the root also of might, main, and dismay.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 4:35
Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him.
Luke 1:4
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
Acts 9:17

And Ananias went his way, and entered into the house; and putting his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mightest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Ghost.
1 Timothy 1:18
This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare;
corruption_summary: Luke 1:4 says the Gospel was written so that its reader might know the certainty of what he had been taught, and the modern instinct that treats certainty about Christian claims as arrogance sets that stated purpose aside.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke is explicit about method and aim. He had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, he consulted eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word, he wrote in order, and he did it so that Theophilus mightest know the certainty. That is a historian’s claim and it invites examination. Against it stands the now-common assumption that religious knowledge is a different species of knowledge, warm but unverifiable, and that anyone claiming certainty about the resurrection has confused faith with evidence. The New Testament does not agree. Paul names witnesses and challenges his readers to go and ask them; Peter denies that the apostles followed cunningly devised fables; John writes so that his readers may know that ye have eternal life. Certainty is the stated goal, and humility about oneself is not the same thing as agnosticism about Christ.

Deuteronomy 4:35 guards the same ground from the other side. The plagues, the sea, the mountain and the voice were shown to Israel for a stated reason: that thou mightest know that the LORD he is God; there is none else beside him. Modern religious pluralism reverses this, treating the exclusive claim as the offensive part and the experience as the acceptable residue. But the exclusivity is the point of the demonstration; a God who is one among several would not need the Red Sea to establish it. 1 Timothy 1:18 adds the practical note that keeps knowledge from turning into mere possession: the prophecies were given Timothy so that he might fight with them. Doctrine held and not used for war is doctrine half received.
roots_summary: Greek hina (G2443), in order that — the purpose conjunction the KJV renders with that…mightest; dunamai (G1410), to be able; Hebrew lemaan (H4616), to the intent that, for the sake of.
roots_lines: Greek hina (G2443) — in order that; the purpose particle behind most New Testament that thou mightest clauses.
Greek hopos (G3704) — so that, to the end that; the near synonym of hina in purpose constructions.
Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; the root of dunamis, power, and the English dynamic.
Hebrew lemaan (H4616) — to the intent that, for the sake of; that thou mightest know in Deuteronomy 4:35.
Greek asphaleia (G803) — certainty, safety, that which cannot be made to slip; Luke’s stated aim in Luke 1:4.
usage: That thou mightest know that the LORD he is God (Deuteronomy 4:35) — the purpose of the whole exodus display.
That thou mightest know the certainty (Luke 1:4) — a historian’s stated aim in writing a Gospel.
That thou by them mightest war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18) — gifts given for a campaign, not for comfort.

etymology: The second-person singular past of know, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it as the form used with thou. In the Gospels it usually appears in an accusation or a lament: the man knew, and did not act on what he knew.
biblical_def: Knewest in the Gospels is almost always the word of judgment, because Scripture treats knowledge as a debt. The unprofitable servant is condemned out of his own defence: Thou wicked and slothful servant, thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed (Matthew 25:26). His excuse becomes his sentence; if he really believed the master severe, that belief obliged him to at least put the money to the exchangers. Over Jerusalem the Lord weeps and gives the reason for the coming ruin in a single clause: they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation (Luke 19:44). Not knowing is here a culpable failure, since the visitation was standing in the road weeping. To the woman at the well the same form opens the door instead of closing it: If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water (John 4:10) — ignorance named, and immediately supplied. And in the psalm the word is a comfort rather than a charge: When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path (Psalm 142:3), spoken by David in a cave. What he could not see, God already knew.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives KNEWEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb know, used with thou: didst perceive with certainty, didst understand, didst recognize or be acquainted with.
webster_full: KNEWEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb KNOW; used with the pronoun thou.
KNOW, v.t. — To perceive with certainty; to understand clearly; to have a clear and certain perception of truth, fact, or existence.
To be acquainted with; to be no stranger to; as, to know a person or a place.
To recognize; to distinguish; and in Scripture, to acknowledge with approbation, as when the Lord knoweth them that are his.
From Saxon cnawan, to know — the root also of acknowledge, cunning in its older sense of skill, and ken.
scriptures: Matthew 25:26
His lord answered and said unto him, Thou wicked and slothful servant, thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed:
Luke 19:44
And shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
John 4:10
Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.
Psalm 142:3
When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path. In the way wherein I walked have they privily laid a snare for me.
corruption_summary: The modern assumption that ignorance excuses is directly reversed in Luke 19:44, where a city is destroyed precisely because it did not know the time of its visitation, and the plea of not knowing is treated as guilt rather than defence.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture distinguishes degrees of guilt by knowledge — that servant, which knew his lord’s will, and prepared not himself… shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47) — but it nowhere treats ignorance as innocence. Romans 1 says the nations are without excuse though they never had Moses, because what may be known of God is manifest in the creation and they held the truth in unrighteousness. Luke 19:44 pronounces judgment on a city for not knowing what was standing in front of it. The popular idea that a person who has not heard, or has not understood, is thereby safe would make evangelism a cruelty rather than a mercy, and the apostles who went to the nations plainly did not believe it.

Matthew 25:26 exposes the more subtle version, in which a low view of God is offered as the reason for doing nothing. The servant calls his lord a hard man who reaps where he did not sow, and buries the talent in fear. The lord does not accept the description, but he does hold the man to it: if that were true, the money should at least have gone to the bankers. A professed conviction that God is severe, exacting, or arbitrary is never a warrant for inaction; it is an argument for greater diligence. And John 4:10 shows the other side, where the Lord meets real ignorance with instruction rather than condemnation — If thou knewest the gift of God — which is the pattern for dealing with the uninformed rather than the willfully unknowing.
roots_summary: Hebrew yada (H3045), to know, by experience and by relationship; Greek ginosko (G1097), to come to know; oida (G1492), to know as a settled possession; episkope (G1984), visitation, the thing Jerusalem failed to know.
roots_lines: Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; covers factual knowledge, experiential knowledge, and covenant intimacy (Amos 3:2).
Greek ginosko (G1097) — to come to know, to learn; the process of knowledge rather than its settled state.
Greek oida (G1492) — to know as a possession already held; the perfect of eido, to see, and so knowledge from having seen.
Greek episkope (G1984) — a visitation, an overseeing; the time of thy visitation (Luke 19:44).
Greek agnoia (G52) — ignorance; the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent (Acts 17:30).
usage: Thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not (Matthew 25:26) — a servant condemned out of his own defence.
Because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation (Luke 19:44) — ignorance as the ground of judgment.
Then thou knewest my path (Psalm 142:3) — what the sufferer could not see, God already knew.

etymology: The second-person singular past of hear, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it as the form used with thou. Scripture uses it in both directions: of God hearing a man’s cry, and of a man having heard God’s word and being answerable for it.
biblical_def: Heardest runs both ways in Scripture, and both are consoling in their own manner. Godward it is the language of answered prayer: For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee (Psalm 31:22). The psalmist confesses that his despairing conclusion was simply wrong; he was never cut off, and the hearing was going on while he believed it was not. Nehemiah’s national confession rehearses the same mercy at the beginning of the nation’s history: And didst see the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heardest their cry by the Red sea (Nehemiah 9:9). Manward, the word measures responsibility. God commends Josiah for what happened in him when the recovered book was read: Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD, when thou heardest what I spake against this place… and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the LORD (2 Kings 22:19) — and the last clause turns the word back Godward, hearing answered by hearing. Caleb appeals to what Joshua had heard forty-five years earlier and asks for the hardest ground in Canaan on the strength of it: thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there, and that the cities were great and fenced (Joshua 14:12).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives HEARDEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb hear, used with thou: didst perceive by the ear; didst listen to; didst attend to; and, of God, didst regard and answer, as prayer.
webster_full: HEARDEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb HEAR; used with the pronoun thou.
HEAR, v.t. — To perceive by the ear; to feel an impression of sound by the proper organs.
To give audience or allowance to speak; to listen to; to attend to.
To regard; to attend to with favour; and hence, of God, to answer — as, the LORD heard my supplication.
From Saxon hyran, to hear — the root also of hearken, hearing, and the older hearsay.
scriptures: Psalm 31:22
For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee.
Nehemiah 9:9
And didst see the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heardest their cry by the Red sea;
2 Kings 22:19

Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD, when thou heardest what I spake against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the LORD.
Joshua 14:12

Now therefore give me this mountain, whereof the LORD spake in that day; for thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there, and that the cities were great and fenced: if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out, as the LORD said.
corruption_summary: Josiah’s response to hearing the Word — a tender heart, humbling, rent clothes and weeping — is the reaction Scripture commends, and the modern habit of hearing preaching as content consumed rather than as God speaking has largely retired it.
corruption_paragraphs: The book found in the temple had been lost long enough that a reigning king did not know what was in it, and when it was read he tore his clothes. God’s commendation in 2 Kings 22:19 lists four things in order: a tender heart, self-humbling, torn clothes, and weeping — and then adds I also have heard thee. That is the biblical shape of hearing the Word: it produces grief, and the grief is itself heard. Set against it, the ordinary modern posture toward preaching is evaluative — the sermon is judged for interest, usefulness, or delivery, and the hearer leaves with an opinion rather than a wound. A congregation may be highly informed and never once tender, and Josiah’s reformation began at the point where the two diverge.

Psalm 31:22 addresses the opposite failure, which is a real one and not to be scolded away. The psalmist said in his haste that he was cut off from God’s eyes, and he was mistaken; the hearing was happening the whole time. Scripture is unembarrassed to record a saint’s despairing verdict on his own case and then correct it, which is why the psalms remain the church’s book for the worst weeks. Note the order: he does not first feel heard and then believe it. He learns afterward that he was heard, and writes the psalm so that the next sufferer may know it earlier. Joshua 14:12 shows a third use — Caleb asking for the hill country of the giants precisely because Joshua had heard the report and knew what it cost.
roots_summary: Hebrew shama (H8085), to hear, to listen, to obey; azan (H238), to give ear; Greek akouo (G191), to hear; eisakouo (G1522), to hear favourably, to answer.
roots_lines: Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, and by extension to obey; the first word of the Shema, Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4).
Hebrew azan (H238) — to give ear, to listen closely; formed from ozen, the ear.
Greek akouo (G191) — to hear; faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17).
Greek eisakouo (G1522) — to hear so as to answer; used of God answering prayer (Matthew 6:7; Hebrews 5:7).
Greek hupakouo (G5219) — to hear under, to obey; the New Testament word for obedience is a hearing word.
usage: Thou heardest the voice of my supplications (Psalm 31:22) — the hearing was going on while he believed it was not.
When thou heardest what I spake against this place (2 Kings 22:19) — the commended reaction to the Word: tenderness, humbling, grief.
Thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there (Joshua 14:12) — Caleb asking for the hardest ground on the strength of what was heard.
